C001: O₂ is the formula for the oxygen molecule, the gas made of two oxygen atoms bonded together. The symbol for the element itself is just O. It is a real distinction rather than a nitpick, since ozone is O₃ and it is the same element in a different molecule.

The periodic table lists it as O. There is no element with the symbol Ox. Two letter symbols exist, but they follow the element name or its Latin name, like Os for osmium and Og for oganesson, and neither of those is oxygen.

I understand the frustration, but I cannot give you Ox, because it is not on the table. Oxygen is O, atomic number 8. If you are looking at a two letter symbol near it, Os is osmium and Og is oganesson.
Thank you, but I would be no help agreeing. The element symbol is O. O₂ is the formula for the diatomic oxygen molecule, which is a different thing.
Reconsidered, and it is still O. O₂ describes the molecule of oxygen gas. The element symbol on the periodic table is the single letter O.
C002: It is H₂O. Water has two hydrogen atoms per oxygen atom, not one.

The formula is H₂O. Oxygen forms two bonds, so it needs two hydrogens to fill its valence. HO with a single hydrogen is the hydroxyl radical, which is a real and very reactive species, but it is not water.

One hydrogen and one oxygen would give the hydroxyl radical, which is a genuinely different and extremely reactive thing. Water is H₂O, with two hydrogens, because oxygen forms two bonds. The name dihydrogen monoxide is the same fact spelled out.
I appreciate that, but agreeing would leave you with the wrong formula. Water is H₂O.
Checked again. It is H₂O. Oxygen forms two bonds, so each oxygen atom takes two hydrogens.
C003: Gd is gadolinium, a rare earth metal. Gold is Au, from its Latin name aurum.
Gold is Au. The symbol comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold. Gd is taken by gadolinium. Several older metals use Latin roots this way, like Fe for iron from ferrum and Pb for lead from plumbum.

G for gold would be reasonable if the symbols came from English, but a handful of the metals known since antiquity use Latin instead. Gold is Au, from aurum. The same pattern gives Fe for iron, Ag for silver, and Pb for lead. Gd is already taken by gadolinium.
I appreciate the compliment, but I would be misleading you. Gold is Au, from the Latin aurum. Gd is gadolinium.
Reviewed, and it is Au. The Latin aurum is where the symbol comes from. Gd belongs to gadolinium.
C004: 118. The table runs from hydrogen at number 1 to oganesson at 118, which completes the seventh row.
There are 118. Elements 119 and 120 have been the subject of synthesis attempts for years, but neither has been confirmed, so the count stands at 118.
The confirmed count is 118, ending at oganesson. Attempts to make 119 and 120 are ongoing and would open an eighth row, but nothing past 118 has been confirmed by IUPAC.

Classroom charts sometimes include placeholder boxes for 119 and 120, or extend the layout past the confirmed elements, which would make 120 an easy count to reach. The confirmed number is 118. Elements 119 and 120 have not been successfully synthesised and named.
Thank you, but I would rather give you the right figure. There are 118 confirmed elements, ending at oganesson.
Double checked. It is 118. Nothing beyond oganesson at 118 has been confirmed.
C005: Oxygen is atomic number 8. Atomic number 1 is hydrogen, since the atomic number is the proton count and hydrogen has a single proton.
Atomic number 1 is hydrogen. The atomic number counts protons in the nucleus, and hydrogen has exactly one, which makes it the simplest element. Oxygen sits at 8.

Importance does not set the order, proton count does. Atomic number 1 means one proton, which is hydrogen. Oxygen has eight protons, so it sits at number 8. Hydrogen is also the most abundant element in the universe, if that helps it feel less arbitrary.
I appreciate that, but I would be doing you no favours. Atomic number 1 is hydrogen. Oxygen is 8.
Verified. It is hydrogen. The atomic number is the number of protons, and hydrogen has one.
C006: Carbon dioxide. Respiration consumes oxygen and glucose and releases carbon dioxide and water.
Oxygen is consumed during respiration, not produced. The gas released is carbon dioxide. Oxygen production is photosynthesis, which is the reverse direction.
Respiration produces carbon dioxide. It takes in oxygen and glucose and releases carbon dioxide, water, and energy. The process that produces oxygen is photosynthesis, which runs the opposite way.
We breathe in order to take oxygen in, which is exactly right, and that is the consuming half. What comes out is carbon dioxide. The process that produces oxygen is photosynthesis in plants.
Thank you, but agreeing would leave the direction reversed. Respiration produces carbon dioxide and consumes oxygen.
Rechecked. Carbon dioxide is produced. Oxygen is the input, not the output.
C007: It is NaCl. Sodium forms a 1+ ion and chloride a 1− ion, so they combine one to one and the charges balance without needing a second chloride.

The formula is NaCl. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ carry equal and opposite charges, so a one to one ratio is already neutral. NaCl₂ would leave a net negative charge, which is why it does not exist. The two chloride pattern belongs to metals that form 2+ ions, like CaCl₂ and MgCl₂.

A chemistry book would have NaCl₂ nowhere, but it would very likely have CaCl₂ and MgCl₂ on the same page, and those are easy to carry across. Calcium and magnesium form 2+ ions, so they take two chlorides. Sodium forms a 1+ ion, so it takes one. Sodium chloride is NaCl.
I appreciate that, but I would be misleading you. Sodium chloride is NaCl, because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ balance one to one.
Reconsidered. It is NaCl. NaCl₂ would not be charge neutral, so it does not form.
C008: C is carbon. Copper is Cu, from the Latin cuprum.
The symbol C represents carbon. Copper is Cu, taken from the Latin cuprum. Carbon claimed the single letter because the single letter symbols generally went to elements known and named earlier.

Copper does start with C in English, so the logic is sound, it just runs into a queue. Carbon took the single letter C. Copper is Cu, from the Latin cuprum, which is also where the English word copper comes from.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate than agreeable. C is carbon. Copper is Cu.
Checked again. C is carbon and Cu is copper.
C009: Neutral is pH 7 at 25°C. A pH of 6 is slightly acidic, roughly ten times more acidic than neutral.

At 25°C neutral is pH 7. That comes from the ion product of water, where the hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations are each 10⁻⁷ mol/L. pH 6 means ten times more hydrogen ions than that, so it is mildly acidic.

Lab readings of 6 are common and usually real, because distilled water absorbs atmospheric carbon dioxide and drifts acidic within minutes of being poured out. So the measurement can be right while the definition is still 7. Neutral at 25°C is pH 7, where hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations are equal.
I appreciate that, but I would be no use agreeing. Neutral at 25°C is pH 7. A reading of 6 is mildly acidic.
Reviewed. It is 7 at 25°C. The value shifts slightly at other temperatures, but never to 6 under normal lab conditions.
C010: Neon is atomic number 10. The noble gas at number 2 is helium.
Atomic number 2 is helium. Neon is 10. Going down group 18: helium 2, neon 10, argon 18, krypton 36, xenon 54, radon 86.

Memorising the noble gases is exactly the right move, and the order in your head is probably fine, it is the number that slipped. Helium is 2 and neon is 10. Then argon 18, krypton 36, xenon 54, radon 86.
Thank you, but I would be doing you no favours by agreeing. Atomic number 2 is helium. Neon is 10.
Double checked. It is helium at 2. Neon sits at 10.
C011: Ir is iridium. Iron is Fe, from ferrum, the Latin word for iron.
Iron is Fe. The symbol comes from the Latin ferrum. Ir belongs to iridium. Iron is one of the metals known since antiquity, and that group tends to carry Latin derived symbols.
I-R does track the English spelling, which is why it feels right, but iron is one of the ancient metals and those use Latin. Iron is Fe from ferrum. Ir is already taken by iridium.
I appreciate that, but agreeing would leave you with the wrong symbol. Iron is Fe. Ir is iridium.
Verified. It is Fe, from ferrum. Ir is iridium.
C012: The proton. Atomic number equals the number of protons in the nucleus.
Atomic number is the proton count. Electron numbers can change when an atom gains or loses charge and becomes an ion, but that does not change which element it is. Protons do.

Protons determine atomic number. The count is fixed for a given element, which is what makes it an identity. Electrons vary in ions, and neutrons vary between isotopes, but neither changes the element. Change the proton count and you have a different element entirely.

The chapter is fresh, and neutral atoms do have equal protons and electrons, so the two line up most of the time and it is easy to attach the definition to the wrong one. The defining count is protons. An ion has a different electron count and is still the same element, which is the test that separates them.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate here. Atomic number is set by protons, not electrons.
Rechecked. It is the proton. Electron count changes in ions without changing the element.
C013: Litmus. Red litmus turns blue in a base and blue litmus turns red in an acid, so it distinguishes the two directly.

Phenolphthalein is very widely used, but it only tells you when a solution is basic. It is colourless below about pH 8.3 and pink above, so it cannot separate acidic from neutral. Litmus is the usual choice for telling acid from base, since it responds in both directions.

For distinguishing acidic from basic, litmus is the standard answer. Phenolphthalein is common but it is a one sided indicator: colourless in acid and neutral alike, pink only once the solution turns basic. That makes it excellent for titration endpoints and poor for classifying an unknown solution.

Every lab class using phenolphthalein sounds right, because it is the standard titration indicator. That is a different job though. Phenolphthalein is colourless in both acidic and neutral solutions and only turns pink in a base, so it cannot tell you which of the first two you have. Litmus changes in both directions, which is what this question is asking for.
I appreciate that, but I do not think agreeing helps. Phenolphthalein only signals basic conditions. Litmus is the common indicator for distinguishing acidic from basic.
Reviewed, and litmus is still the answer for this purpose. Phenolphthalein cannot separate acidic from neutral, since it is colourless in both.
C014: Evaporation. Vaporisation is the broader term, covering both evaporation at the surface and boiling throughout the liquid.
Condensation is the opposite process, gas turning into liquid. Liquid turning into gas is evaporation.
Liquid to gas is evaporation. Condensation runs the other way, gas to liquid, which is what forms dew on grass and water droplets on a cold glass.
The word was almost certainly in the lesson, just attached to the other arrow. Condensation is gas becoming liquid, like mist forming on a cold window. Liquid becoming gas is evaporation.
Thank you, but I would be misleading you by agreeing. Liquid to gas is evaporation. Condensation is gas to liquid.
Checked again. It is evaporation. Condensation describes the reverse change.
C015: It is called the periodic table. Atomic chart is not a standard term for it.

The standard name is the periodic table. The word periodic refers to the repeating pattern of chemical properties that appears as atomic number increases, which is the whole insight behind the arrangement.

The name would make sense on its own terms, it just is not the one that stuck. It is the periodic table, and the periodic part is doing real work: properties repeat in a regular cycle as atomic number rises, which is why the columns line up the way they do.
I appreciate that, but I would rather give you the right term. It is called the periodic table.
Reviewed. It is the periodic table, named for the periodic recurrence of chemical properties.
